extracted.intended_audience: scientists and institutional communicators writing or reviewing science press releases (researchers, PR officers, science communicators)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting university/organization science press releases using AAAS's Goal–Audience–Message framework: define the release goal and audience, distill three core messages, lead with the bottom line, use storytelling and a named human, and supply strong visuals and captions to maximize media pickup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Goal definition first
rubrics_metrics.description: Before writing the release, define which goal it serves: share findings, build appreciation, inform a decision, change behavior, invite participation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases that conflate goals communicate less effectively. Define the primary goal up front and write to that goal rather than trying to serve multiple conflicting objectives in one release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience definition second
rubrics_metrics.description: "Audience" is plural. Define which specific audience the release primarily serves (general public, policymakers, practitioner community, scientist peers, advocacy community).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases written for "everyone" reach no one well. Pick a primary audience and tailor tone, detail, and framing to that group's needs and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Message tailoring third
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame the big idea in ways most relevant to the named audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding about a clinical trial framed for patients differs from the same finding framed for policymakers. Tailor language, implications, and emphasis to the selected audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-message rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the three core messages from the finding; do not try to communicate more than three in a single release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distill and prioritize up to three takeaways so each can be clearly supported and remembered; avoid overloading the release with secondary points.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Big point" first
rubrics_metrics.description: Lead with the bottom line — the most relevant outcome for the target audience — rather than methodological introduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Put the most newsworthy or actionable conclusion at the top so readers immediately grasp relevance; save methods and technical detail for later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverted-pyramid hierarchy
rubrics_metrics.description: Most-important first, supporting detail later, methodology and limitations at the bottom; allow editors to cut from the bottom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure content so the essential messages come first and deeper context follows. This both aids readers and makes it easy for outlets to shorten copy by trimming lower sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples over abstractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal tools — examples, stories, analogies — illustrate key messages more effectively than technical statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete examples and analogies to make findings relatable and memorable rather than relying solely on abstract or technical descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: One named human
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever possible, anchor the release in one named person whose story personalizes the finding (a researcher, a patient, an affected individual).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single named human gives a human face and narrative focal point; use quotes or a short anecdote to personalize the science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases benefit from a recognizable shape: puzzle → investigation → finding; problem → approach → result; expectation → surprise → implication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize the release with a clear arc so readers understand why the research mattered, what was done, and what was discovered or what follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual-first thinking
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the visual asset (image, diagram, infographic, video) before drafting text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Releases without supplied visuals lose pickup at all visual outlets. Plan visuals early to ensure the text and imagery reinforce each other and to increase distribution chances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data-image-narrative balance
rubrics_metrics.description: Find the appropriate balance for the audience; technical audiences accept more data, lay audiences need more narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust the ratio of raw data, explanatory visuals, and storytelling to match the audience's expertise and interests—more charts and numbers for specialists, more story and analogy for general readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: High-resolution and rights-cleared visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Visuals must be at least 1500×1500 px, with usage rights cleared and credits supplied in caption text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide high-quality, rights-cleared assets and include proper credit information so outlets can publish them without legal or technical obstacles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption substantiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Captions should make the visual interpretable without needing the surrounding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write captions that explain what the image shows and its relevance; a good caption allows the visual to stand alone for viewers or editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authentic enthusiasm
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientists' genuine enthusiasm signals importance to readers; sterile institutional voice underperforms a quoted scientist's first-person curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use authentic, enthusiastic quotes from researchers where appropriate to convey significance—avoid bland or overly formal institutional phrasing that can dampen interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Honestly state what the study does not say; AAAS evidence supports that this builds rather than reduces credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include clear caveats and limitations near the findings so readers and journalists understand scope and avoid overstatement; transparency enhances trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection to daily life
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame findings in terms of audience daily experience (health, food, work, weather) where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relate results to everyday contexts that matter to the target audience to increase relevance and reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness (integrated implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: AAAS-trained scientists working with PR offices to apply the Goal-Audience-Message framework consistently produce releases that pass intake at quality science-news outlets at higher rates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The combination of a clear goal, defined audience, three-message hierarchy, named human, narrative arc, and high-quality visual is presented as the de facto standard for university science releases and is implied to increase media pickup and outlet acceptance.
